name: Six Flags Entertainment Corporation

profile.description: Six Flags Entertainment Corporation is the largest regional theme park operator in North America, formed by the July 2024 merger of Cedar Fair and Six Flags. The company operates 35 amusement, water, and family entertainment parks (42 pre-divestiture) across the US, Canada, and Mexico, attracting 47.4M guests in 2025 with $61.90 per capita spending. Seven parks were divested to EPR Properties in March 2026 for $331M.

innovation.label: WEAK
innovation.analysis: Track Record (1/3): The Cedar Fair/Six Flags merger closed July 2024 creating the largest North American regional park operator, but integration has been challenging — 2025 revenue of $3.1B included a $1.5B non-cash goodwill impairment signaling the combined entity's value fell short of acquisition assumptions [1]. Q1 2026 showed improvement with revenue up 12% YoY to $225.6M, attendance up 4% to 2.9M visits, and per capita spending up 6% to $69.26, but this is recovery, not innovation [2]. AI Deployment (0/2): No AI products, AI-driven revenue, or specific quantified AI operational savings disclosed. Market Share (1/2): Largest regional theme park operator by attendance (47.4M guests FY2025) and park count, but loses share to Disney, Universal, and SeaWorld in the broader destination/experience economy [1]. Product Pipeline (1/2): Ongoing investment in family-oriented attractions, F&B upgrades, and new roller coasters for 2026 season, but these are standard seasonal additions without specific revenue targets or transformative product innovations [3]. R&D Intensity (0/1): Theme parks do not conduct traditional R&D; capital expenditure goes to ride engineering and park maintenance.

inspiration.label: WEAK
inspiration.analysis: Mission Floor (2/4): Six Flags' mission centers on delivering 'memorable family entertainment and shared experiences' — clear and authentic but interchangeable with any theme park operator, from SeaWorld to Merlin Entertainments [3]. Community Impact (1/2): Six Flags Magic Mountain is building California's largest single-site commercial solar project (12.37 MW capacity) to achieve energy self-sufficiency, a distinctive environmental investment aligned with community values [4]. Standard local community engagement programs at park locations. Employee Retention (0/2): 4,225 full-time employees operate 35+ parks, indicating heavy reliance on seasonal workers. Glassdoor reviews cite strict policies, write-ups for minor infractions, and seasonal workforce challenges. CEO John Reilly (December 2025) launched an employee feedback channel receiving 300+ submissions and conducts field visits, but these efforts are nascent [3]. Insider Buying (0/2): No meaningful net insider buying identified. CEO Reilly received standard executive equity grants upon appointment.

infrastructure.label: WEAK
infrastructure.analysis: Mechanically scored on available metrics — severely impacted by post-merger leverage and GAAP impairment charges. D/E of 1076% ($5.53B debt vs. $117M cash) is far above the 300% floor, scoring 0 [5]. ROE of -123.4% and profit margin of -52.75% both score 0, driven by the $1.5B non-cash goodwill impairment in FY2025 [1]. Revenue growth YoY of 12% (Q1 2026) is the sole positive metric, scoring near target [2]. Forward P/E and PEG are unavailable due to GAAP losses. Altman Z-Score of 0.31 indicates bankruptcy risk. Free cash flow of just $28.7M TTM on $3.12B revenue demonstrates minimal cash generation capacity after debt service [5]. Liquidity floor passes: 2.43M avg volume x $18.92 = $45.9M.

ai_resilience.label: LOW RISK
ai_resilience.analysis: AI Risk Protection (8/9): Theme parks are the quintessential physical-experience business that AI structurally cannot replace — riding a roller coaster, sharing a family day at an amusement park, and in-person entertainment are experiential products beyond AI's reach [3]. Park real estate, ride engineering, food and beverage operations, and live event programming are all physical-world operations immune to AI substitution. Analysts have not flagged AI as a disruption risk for regional theme parks. The business earns 8 rather than 9 because AI does not directly increase demand for theme parks the way it does for energy or semiconductors. AI Opportunity (0/1): Six Flags generates no quantifiable AI revenue. Internal automation projects are early-stage and not revenue-generating.

infinite_game.summary: Six Flags is in the midst of a difficult merger integration with a new CEO, $5.53B in debt, and a $1.5B goodwill impairment in its first full reporting year. The legacy Cedar Fair brand had genuine operational continuity, but the combined entity's posture is reactive — cost synergies, debt management, and park divestitures dominate the strategic agenda rather than purpose-driven investment. CEO Reilly's employee engagement efforts are promising but nascent.

just_cause.analysis: Just Cause (1/3): Creating shared family entertainment memories is an authentic cause that connects work to a larger purpose, but it is shared across every theme park operator globally and does not differentiate Six Flags from Disney, SeaWorld, or Merlin [3]. The cause did not prevent the company from recording a $1.5B impairment or accumulating $5.53B in debt — financial engineering, not purpose, drove the merger. Sinek would see a company with a nice mission statement but no Just Cause.

trusting_teams.analysis: Trusting Teams (1/2): CEO Reilly launched an internal feedback channel receiving 300+ employee submissions and prioritizes field visits and leadership town halls, demonstrating genuine effort at building psychological safety [3]. However, the seasonal workforce model, Glassdoor reviews citing strict policies and high turnover, and the complete leadership reset (new CEO December 2025, new CMO and CLO June 2026) make this adequate trust at best.

worthy_rivals.analysis: Worthy Rivals (0/1): No specific evidence of an infinite competitive mindset. The Cedar Fair/Six Flags merger itself was a consolidation play to compete with Disney and Universal through scale rather than through learning from these rivals' strengths. Competitive framing focuses on market positioning rather than self-improvement.

existential_flexibility.analysis: Existential Flexibility (1/2): The Cedar Fair/Six Flags merger is a major strategic transformation creating a scaled regional operator, and the subsequent divestiture of 7 parks for $331M to EPR Properties shows willingness to optimize the portfolio [2]. However, these are financial engineering moves — consolidation and asset sales — rather than the kind of business model reinvention that Sinek describes as existential flexibility.

courage_to_lead.analysis: Courage to Lead (1/2): Continuing capital investment in new rides and attractions for the 2026 season despite the $1.5B impairment, declining stock price, and distressed balance sheet shows some willingness to invest through stress [3]. The park divestiture for $331M, while painful, demonstrates willingness to make difficult portfolio decisions. However, the leveraged merger itself created the financial distress — it is difficult to credit as courage what may have been a strategic miscalculation.

investment_thesis: Six Flags is the largest North American regional theme park operator with 35 parks (post-divestiture) drawing 47.4M guests annually and generating $3.1B FY2025 revenue with $792M adjusted EBITDA (25.5% margin) [1]. Q1 2026 showed operational momentum with revenue up 12%, attendance up 4%, and per capita spending up 6% to $69.26, suggesting the post-merger integration is stabilizing [2]. The business is structurally immune to AI disruption, and CEO John Reilly's operational focus on guest experience, employee engagement, and portfolio optimization (divesting 7 parks for $331M) signals disciplined turnaround management [3]. Inspire score of +29 (ALIGNED) with 13 positive attributions and zero negatives provides faith-based appeal.
thesis_continued: The bear case is dominated by the balance sheet. D/E of 1076% ($5.53B debt vs. $117M cash) and an Altman Z-Score of 0.31 place Six Flags in the bankruptcy risk zone [5]. The $1.5B non-cash goodwill impairment in FY2025 effectively acknowledged the merger destroyed value, pushing GAAP profit margin to -52.75% and ROE to -123.4% [1]. Free cash flow of just $28.7M TTM on $3.12B revenue demonstrates that after debt service, the business generates minimal excess cash. Short interest of 18.78% reflects significant market skepticism. The regional theme park industry faces secular headwinds from declining youth attendance, competition from digital entertainment, and rising labor and insurance costs. Until leverage comes down materially and the company demonstrates sustained attendance and per capita spending growth, FUN remains a distressed turnaround with significant downside risk.
key_catalysts: Q1 2026 operational momentum — revenue +12%, attendance +4%, per capita spending +6% to $69.26 — sustaining through the peak summer 2026 season and validating post-merger integration
Park divestitures ($331M from 7 parks to EPR Properties) plus adjusted EBITDA of $792M enabling gradual deleveraging from 1076% D/E toward a more sustainable capital structure
CEO John Reilly executing on guest experience transformation with 30+ years of theme park operations expertise and a fresh operational playbook
key_risks: Capital structure distress — D/E of 1076% with $5.53B debt, Altman Z-Score of 0.31, and only $28.7M TTM free cash flow leaving no margin for operational disappointment or a recession
The $1.5B goodwill impairment acknowledged the Cedar Fair/Six Flags merger destroyed value; further impairments or write-downs remain possible if attendance and pricing fail to recover

Secular headwinds for regional theme parks — declining youth attendance, digital entertainment competition, and rising labor and insurance costs — compounded by 18.78% short interest reflecting active bearish positioning
